title: Leonore’s answer
where: *Fidelio*, Act 2, Scene 5, with Act 1, Scene 6 and Act 2, Scene 3
about: Leonore, dressed as a man and calling herself Fidelio, has taken service with the jailer Rocco to find her husband Florestan, whom the governor Pizarro holds in a dungeon of the state prison. In the first passage Pizarro has just failed to kill him, and husband and wife are alone. The second is her scene alone in Act 1, after she has watched Pizarro and Rocco go off together. The third comes before the first: the moment in the dungeon when she steps between her husband and Pizarro’s dagger.

view.says: No account of this opera by Auden has been found. In a 1947 lecture on *King Lear*, known from students’ notes, he said this of Cordelia. When Lear wakes and says she has cause not to love him, she twice answers that she has none. Compare, Auden said, Leonore’s answer to Florestan.
view.quote: Cordelia wants to love freely, without compulsion, and paradoxically she describes love as a duty.
view.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), pp. 225–26
view.checked: read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned book at the Internet Archive (item lecturesonshakes00aude, which can only be borrowed) through its full-text search; the searches are listed in notes.md. The quoted sentence came back whole across two snippets (the searches "wants to love freely" and "love as a duty"). The running head "226 KING LEAR" falls between Lear’s lines on waking and Cordelia’s answer. In this book a head stands at the top of its page: the editor’s textual note on the comparison is keyed to p. 226 and the index gives Fidelio at 226, and the comparison follows that head. So the comparison with Leonora and the sentence on authority are on p. 226 (the page the research notes give, C section 28 and appendix H16), and the quoted sentence, a few lines before the head, is on p. 225. The research notes and the lead in pieces.json connect the comparison with Cordelia’s "Nothing" in Act 1, Scene 1: the snippets show it is with her answer in Act 4, Scene 7.

lenses.label: Versions

ties.say: In the German Florestan exclaims twice: true wife, woman without equal. The shortened text keeps the first.
Her reason: her soul was with him, and she asks how her body could not have felt strong, fighting for its better self. The shortened text has none of this. Its next word is the first cry of the duet.
The German calls the suffering unnameable. The English calls it *great*.
The German calls the delight very great. The English calls it *past utterance*: the two descriptions have changed places.

lenses.caption: In the German libretto, printed here with its spoken dialogue uncut, Leonore says Nichts, nothing, once, and then gives a reason. Two American librettos print a shortened German text at this point, with the word twice and no reason, and the English shown here follows it. A word said again at once, with nothing between, is the figure of emphasis called epizeuxis. The students’ notes of Auden’s lecture give her answer in this doubled form. He set it beside Cordelia’s No cause, no cause, her reply when Lear, waking, says she has cause not to love him. Cordelia, Auden said, has no wish for authority; she wants her love to be free.
lenses.why: In the shortened text of two American librettos Leonore’s answer has lost its reason and is a denial said twice, which is how the notes of Auden’s lecture give it, beside Cordelia’s twice-said denial of any cause.

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: Each spoken speech opens with an exclamation and then comes to a sentence with its verb: hast … erduldet, have borne; war, was; hätte … gefühlt, would have felt; kämpfte, fought. Leonore’s last sentence is a question that argues. After the heading Duett the six lines shown have no verb: they name joy, husband, breast, Leonore, suffering, delight. The whole duet, eighteen lines, has three verbs, each a form of to be. Auden called the sensible passages of a libretto conversation, not song, and held that what is written for singing cannot be poetry: poetry reflects, and will not rest in the outcries of feeling, while music is immediate.
lenses.why: In these lines the sentences that reason are spoken and the six sung lines are exclamations without a verb; Auden called a libretto’s sensible passages conversation, not song, and held that verses for singing cannot be poetry.

lenses.caption: Namenlose is nameless and unnennbarem unnameable: the sung lines say that this joy and that suffering are beyond naming. Adelung’s dictionary, in a volume of 1798, gives namenlos in this sense to the higher style of the moderns: what cannot be named or expressed because of its amount or its intensity. Twelve lines of the libretto have one of three such words, these two or unaussprechlich, unspeakable, and eleven are sung. The twelfth is Leonore’s, spoken in the dungeon shortly before her husband turns his face to her. The right plot for a libretto, Auden wrote, is melodrama: it sets its people in situations too strange or too tragic for words.
lenses.why: Where speech gives way to song the words themselves say that the feeling cannot be named, and eleven of the libretto’s twelve such lines are sung; Auden held that a good libretto puts its people where words fail.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: four beats to the line in the recitative; four and three by turns in the lines to Hope; three, two, two and three in the four lines after them

points.say: The outcry is one word of four syllables with a single stress. The measure’s second beat falls on its last syllable, and the voice passes over it.
A question, with its verb first: the line can open on two stresses side by side. It can also be said with the first of them light.
Seven more lines of the recitative, all of four beats, are left out above this heading: in them she turns from his rage to her own calm. Inside the recitative the score changes speed several times.
A command, a pause, and the name of the one she calls: the line opens on two stresses.
Two beats and a complete statement: I do not waver. The next line has two beats as well, and its sentence runs on into the last line.
The aria has eight more lines: four to her husband, in the measure of the lines to Hope, and then these last four again.

lenses.caption: The line begins off the beat throughout, with a beat on every second syllable. The recitative, the declaimed opening, has four beats to the line and begins as a speech to the man who has just left. Under the heading Arie the lines shown go four, three, four, three, and then three, two, two, three. At the first change she calls on Hoffnung, Hope; at the second she says Ich, I. Beethoven’s music divides at the same places: Adagio, very slow, at the first, and Allegro con brio, quick, with life and fire, at the second. Auden held that a librettist’s verses are written to the composer, not the public, as a private letter is.
lenses.why: The measure changes where Leonore begins to call on Hope and where she states her own resolve, and Beethoven’s music divides at the same two places; Auden called a librettist’s verses a letter for the composer, not for the public.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The four lines of recitative shown rhyme from the outside in: hin waits two lines for Tigersinn, while Grimme is answered at once by Stimme. The lines to Hope rhyme by turns. The last four close in again around the two short lines, which end on wanke nicht, do not waver, and die Pflicht, duty. In a stanza so rhymed, a handbook of English verse says, the third line’s rhyme gains emphasis from its nearness to the second: here that word is duty. Around the pair, Triebe, drive, waits for Gattenliebe, married love. Adelung’s dictionary, in a volume of 1801, noted that poets often use Trieb for love, for the convenience of the rhyme.
lenses.why: The enclosing rhyme puts the two short lines at the center, gives duty the emphasis of a rhyme that returns at once, and rhymes her drive with married love; poets, Adelung notes, used Trieb as a rhyme word for love.

grounds.claim: the rhyme scheme of the twelve lines: enclosed in the four lines of recitative, alternate in the lines to Hope, enclosed in the last four with the two short lines as the inner pair
in the stanza rhymed abba the rhyme of the third line receives increased emphasis from its proximity to that of the second
grounds.source: Paull F. Baum, The Principles of English Versification (1922), chapter 4, on the In Memoriam stanza; the same chapter on the short couplet (the quick return of the rime makes the couplet felt as a unit). The handbook describes English verse

lenses.caption: Her resolve names two grounds. Triebe is a drive: Adelung’s dictionary, in a volume of 1801, defines Trieb as a bent of a living creature’s force, commonly one that does not come merely from our own purpose. Pflicht is duty: in the same dictionary a thing commanded, and also a sworn promise of fidelity. Rocco, who uses the word most often, says what he means by it: carrying out the orders he is given. Leonore’s is the duty of Gattenliebe, married love.
lenses.why: Leonore gives her resolve two grounds, an inner drive and the duty of married love; Adelung’s dictionary gives the senses the two words then had, and Rocco, who says duty most often, means by it carrying out orders.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: One word in each. The German makes a name for the man out of an adjective, abominable; the English has *Monster*.
The German has an image: the last star of the weary, which must not grow pale. The English has no star: a *lingering heart* here, and a *ray of joy* in its next line.
For the inner drive the English has a beating bosom.
Kept: I do not waver, *I hesitate not*.
In the German duty strengthens her. The English has no word for duty: she brings *fresh vigor* herself.
True married love becomes *a wife devout*.

lenses.caption: The English comes from a New York libretto that names no translator. It has six lines for these twelve, each of ten to sixteen syllables, so the measures are gone, and it has no rhyme. It keeps the outcry and drops the two nouns of the resolve: Triebe, drive, and Pflicht, duty. Auden believed that a listener to song hears syllables, not words, and that the syllables of the verse decide the composer’s vocal line; for that reason he was, in general, against performing operas in translation.
lenses.why: The English keeps the outcry and the resolve but not the measures, the rhymes or the words for drive and duty; Auden believed listeners to song hear the syllables the composer set, and so was against performing operas in translation.

grounds.claim: the English has six lines for the twelve German lines shown, no rhyme, and neither a word for the drive nor a word for duty; it keeps the outcry and the refusal to waver

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: epistrophe
lenses.plain: the same word at the end of phrase after phrase
lenses.caption: Three speeches in a row end on one word, Weib, wife. Ending one phrase after another on the same word is the figure called epistrophe; here four voices share it. Leonore says the word first, and speaks of herself as she would of someone else: sein, his. Rocco and Pizarro give her last two words back as a question. Florestan changes the first of them to Mein, my: the man she spoke of speaks for himself. Only then does she turn to him with her name, which he repeats, and to the others with Ich bin, I am, and the word a fourth time.
lenses.why: Three speeches by four voices end on the same word while the word before it changes from his to my: Florestan’s answer is the last two words of her cry with one word changed.

grounds.claim: three successive speeches end on the same word; the word before it is his, his, my; then her name stands twice, at the end of her speech and as the whole of his; then the full sentence, with the end word a fourth time
epistrophe is defined there as a run of lines, phrases, clauses or sentences that all close on the same word or words

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: four beats shared among three speeches, then three beats, the name alone, three beats, and four; every line but the name beginning off the beat

points.say: The measure has no beat on this word. A voice that marks the change from *his* to *my* stresses it all the same.
Her name closes a line of three beats. The line that rhymes with it, two lines on, ends on the word for sworn.
The name by itself: four syllables, beginning on a beat.
The measure puts its beat on the second word, *am*. A voice can as fairly stress the first, *I*.

To him comfort, ruin to you: the two men stand at the ends of the phrase and what she has sworn to each in the middle. A voice that sets *him* against *you* stresses the word for *him*, where the measure has no beat.

lenses.caption: Her cry has four syllables, the men’s question two, Florestan’s answer two. Counted together they make eight syllables and four beats, the length of the last line shown, which one voice has to itself: the discovery, from her word to his, takes the space of one such line. Auden wrote of librettos in general that a spoken play can let a mistake come to light slowly, but in opera recognition has to be abrupt, since “song cannot walk, it can only jump.”
lenses.why: The recognition takes eight syllables shared among four voices, the length of the last line shown; Auden held that in a libretto recognition must be abrupt, because song cannot move by slow steps.

lenses.caption: Weib was once the common German word both for a woman and for a wife. Adelung’s dictionary, in a volume of 1801, calls its use restricted: in common life, of humble married or elderly women; in familiar talk, of a wife, more often in Upper Germany, the south, where nothing was more common than mein Weib, my wife; in poetry and the higher style, commonly only of a stout-hearted, manly woman, with a secondary idea of strength. Leonore says it in man’s clothes, between her husband and a dagger. The libretto has the word once before this line, in Jaquino’s wooing of Marzelline. Soon after, Pizarro asks whether he is to tremble before a Weib.
lenses.why: The word in which she says who she is was the familiar word for a wife and, in the higher style of the time, the word for a stout-hearted woman; the libretto has it only once before this line.

grounds.claim: Weib meant a woman and a wife, and was used in both senses in all cases in the Middle Ages; its present use is restricted: in common life of lowly married or elderly women; in familiar speech of a married woman, more often in Upper Germany than in Upper Saxony, and there nothing is commoner than mein Weib for my wife; in poetry and the higher style commonly only of a stout-hearted, manly woman, with a secondary idea of strength
grounds.source: Adelung, Grammatisch-kritisches Wörterbuch, vol. 4 (1801), cols. 1440-41, under Weib, senses 1 and 2 and note 1; DWDS under Weib (the history of the word)

lenses.caption: In Act 1 of the German libretto the heroine is called Fidelio fifteen times and Leonore never: under the name Fidelio Marzelline loves her and Rocco chooses her for a son-in-law. In the dungeon Florestan says Leonore three times before he knows her. In the lines of this passage she says it herself, the only time in the opera, and nobody says Fidelio afterward. Beethoven, Grove’s dictionary says, wished the opera called Leonora. Auden wrote that drama rests on a mistake and that good drama moves in two steps: the mistake is made, then found out. One of his examples, not from this opera, is a chambermaid who is really a young nobleman, disguised.
lenses.why: The mistake the plot turns on is carried by a name: Fidelio is said sixteen times before she names herself Leonore and never after; Auden held that drama rests on a mistake and on its discovery.

auden.says: Auden names the opera once in *The Dyer’s Hand*, and it is the overture he speaks of. Leonora No. 3, he grants, is fine music for a concert; played in the theater between the two scenes of Act 2 of *Fidelio*, it is, he says, acutely boring for all its twelve minutes. His reason is that an opera’s orchestra plays for the singers and not for the listeners. A lover of opera bears an orchestral interlude, and may even like it, so long as he understands that the singers need rest or the scene is being changed; any other playing by the orchestra alone is, to him, time wasted.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 472
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 22225-22235, on 2026-10-03; the running head of p. 472 stands at line 22204. The name Fidelio occurs nowhere else in that scan (searched).

auden.says: In the same notes he writes that drama rests on a mistake; one example is a chambermaid who is really a young nobleman, disguised. A good play moves in two steps: the mistake is made, and then it is found out. In a spoken play the finding out may be slow; in a libretto recognition must be sudden, because music cannot live with uncertainty. The plot a libretto needs, he says, is melodrama: it sets its people in situations too strange or too tragic for words, and a sensible mood is not one for singing. He is writing of librettos in general, not of *Fidelio*.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 471–72

auden.says: Of a libretto’s words he writes that poetry is at bottom reflection: it will not stop at the outcries of feeling as it comes, and tries to understand what is felt. Music is immediate, so what is written to be sung cannot be poetry. A librettist’s verses are meant for the composer, not for the public, as a letter is for one reader, and their great moment is the one in which they give him a melody. A listener to song, he believes, hears syllables and not words, and it is the syllables that decide the vocal line; for that reason he is, in general, against performing operas in translation.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 472–73

caveats: Auden’s remark comes from students’ notes of a lecture of 1947, put together by an editor in 2000, and was read for this page only in short extracts of a library copy. He said it of Cordelia, and told the class only to compare Leonore’s answer.

Leonore’s answer exists in three forms. The uncut German here has the word once, with a reason. A German vocal score (Peters), giving the dialogue as spoken on stage, has it once, with no reason. Two American librettos have it twice in their German; the English shown here follows one.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of the German, and a few syllables could fairly be marked otherwise. The handbook cited for the rhyme describes English verse. The tempo words were read in the Peters vocal score, not in a full score.

The counts of names and words follow the uncut German libretto. The English printed here is a shortened text and has fewer: *Fidelio* fourteen times and *Leonora* nine. That the three short speeches of the third passage fill one line is also a count; the libretto prints them apart.
The glosses are plain modern renderings, and the phrase about the better self can be taken two ways.
open: The lead in pieces.json and the research notes (C section 28, appendix H16) say Auden set Leonore’s words beside Cordelia’s "Nothing". The snippets of the lecture show otherwise: the comparison is with Cordelia’s twice-said denial of cause in Act 4, Scene 7 (Lectures on Shakespeare, p. 226).

Lectures on Shakespeare can only be borrowed at the Internet Archive and was read in full-text-search snippets, not page by page. The page numbers rest on running heads seen in snippets. The head "226 KING LEAR" stands just before Cordelia’s answer and the comparison, and the index gives Fidelio at 226, so in this book a head stands at the top of its page. The quoted sentence stands a few lines before that head, so on p. 225. The editor’s textual note on the place (keyed to p. 226; it quotes the libretto with the word once and reports that the notes of Ansen and of Bodenstein both have it twice) ends just before the head "TEXTUAL NOTES 385", so at the foot of p. 384. The punctuation of the quoted sentence should be checked against a printed copy.

Nothing Auden said about Fidelio in the 1941 class is on record; the view is put together from a 1947 lecture on King Lear and from his notes on opera of 1962, which name Fidelio only for the overture.

The printed Stuttgart edition of 1970 that zeno.org follows was not seen, nor the librettos of 1805, 1806 and 1814. Who wrote which lines (Sonnleithner, Breuning or Treitschke) is known here only from Treitschke’s account as Thayer gives it, and is kept out of the captions.

The Peters vocal score and the Ditson libretto were read in the machine-read text of their scans, not in page images. (From the examiner: the library record dates the score 1888, but the scanned copy spells Tür, Tor, getan, Teil and gibt throughout and never with th or ie. That is the spelling made the rule in 1901, as far as the examiner knows without having opened a source for it, so the copy looks like a later printing; the printed notes now say only that the library dates it 1888. Nothing in the piece turns on the date.) Where exactly the marks Poco adagio, Più moto and Allegro in tempo fall inside the recitative could not be told from that text; the Adagio and the Allegro con brio stand clearly before the call to Hope and before the resolve. Corrected by the examiner: a tempo word does follow the Allegro con brio. The same machine-read text has Più lento at the head of score p. 65, in the second half of the four lines to her husband (the stanza that returns to four and three beats and is not shown), and Tempo I as they end. So that stanza begins in the quick speed and slows in its second half; the caption speaks only of the lines shown, and its two tempo marks stand where it says.

In the German parts cut for this piece every source line is its own block, so speakers’ names, stage directions and the headings of the numbers were rows of the passages. Since 3 October the plate key `stage`, set by the lead, lifts them out of the verse in two passages. In `answer` row 6.0, the heading of the number, is set as a direction and rows 7.0, 10.0 and 13.0 as names (her name, his, and the word for both). In `name` rows 1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0 and 11.0 are names, three of them with a direction; `under` is false there so that the English, whose speeches do not answer the German rows one for one, stands beside the German and not line under line. The word tabs’ glosses of the directions and of the word for both now stand after them. In `scene` rows 0.0 and 12.0, the two headings, are still rows of the passage, because a note of the word tab and the third remark of Beat stand on them; they wait for the kit to set a whole row as a heading. In `answer` the two spoken speeches (rows 4.0 and 5.0) begin with the speaker’s name in capitals; the part was cut from the start of the scene’s dialogue so that the build’s rule for such names applies and sets each name over its row. The part of the third passage was cut one line early so that its first row is not the part’s first row, which the build sets in ordinary case.

That the three short speeches of the third passage make "one line" is a count (four, two and two syllables), not something the libretto prints as one line. Around them the quartet’s lines have six or seven syllables.

Corrected by the examiner: Adelung does have the verb, under the headword "Er-dulden" at zeno.org (vol. 1, 1793, col. 1884), and it is now cited. Gattenliebe is not in Grimm; Tigersinn is not in the DWDS. The inflected forms of the name (Leonoren, Leonorens) were not looked up in a grammar and nothing is said of them.
Baum’s handbook describes English verse; its remark on the stanza rhymed abba is made of four-beat lines, and is applied here to German lines of three, two, two and three beats.
Grove’s statement that Beethoven wished the opera called Leonora dates from 1879; later scholarship on the title was not consulted.

The DWDS glosses are those of a modern dictionary. For the words on which a caption leans (namenlos, unnennbar, Trieb, Pflicht, Weib, wanken, Gatte) Adelung’s dictionary of 1793-1801 was read as well.
